title: Simultaneity And Time Dilation
lead: Two events that are simultaneous for one observer need not be simultaneous for another who moves relative to the first, so simultaneity is not absolute. Elapsed time is not absolute either. A clock moving relative to an observer is measured to run slow, and the time $\kdt$ the observer measures is longer than the proper time $\kdto$ by the factor $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - \kv^2/\kc^2}$, which is very nearly 1 at everyday speeds and grows without limit as $\kv$ approaches $\kc$.
objectives: Compare proper time and the observer’s measured time.
Explain why the twin paradox is a false paradox.
summary_html:
• Two events are defined to be simultaneous if an observer measures them as occurring at the same time. They are not necessarily simultaneous to all observers—simultaneity is not absolute.
  • Time dilation is the phenomenon of time passing slower for an observer who is moving relative to another observer.
  • Observers moving at a relative velocity $\kv$ do not measure the same elapsed time for an event. Proper time $\kdto$ is the time measured by an observer at rest relative to the event being observed. Proper time is related to the time $\kdt$ measured by an Earth-bound observer by the equation $$\kdt=\frac{\kdto}{\sqrt{1-\frac{\kv^{2}}{\kc^{2}}}}=\gamma\kdto,$$ where $$\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{\kv^{2}}{\kc^{2}}}}.$$
  • The equation relating proper time and time measured by an Earth-bound observer implies that relative velocity cannot exceed the speed of light.
  • The twin paradox asks why a twin traveling at a relativistic speed away and then back towards the Earth ages less than the Earth-bound twin. The premise to the paradox is faulty because the traveling twin is accelerating. Special relativity does not apply to accelerating frames of reference.
  • Time dilation is usually negligible at low relative velocities, but it does occur, and it has been verified by experiment.

The book’s own slips are kept as it prints them: the last sentence of the flash-lamp paragraph (“B will measure the light from the right bulb and arrive at observer A before…”) is garbled, “Simultaneity is not absolute.” carries a double stop, and “In the case of the astronaut observe the reflecting light” is the book’s wording. A muon in the Earth’s atmosphere lives longer as measured by an Earth-bound observer than measured by the muon’s internal clock.

The twin paradox asks why the traveling twin ages less than the Earth-bound twin. That is the prediction we obtain if we consider the Earth-bound twin’s frame. In the astronaut’s frame, however, the Earth is moving and time runs slower there. Who is correct?

exercises.prompt: 1. What is $\gamma$ if $\kv=0.650\kc$? 2. A particle travels at $1.90\times 10^{8}\;\text{m/s}$ and lives $2.10\times 10^{-8}\;\text{s}$ when at rest relative to an observer. How long does the particle live as viewed in the laboratory?

parts.hint: The lifetime at rest is the proper time; divide it by $\sqrt{1 - \kv^2/\kc^2}$ with $\kc = 3.00\times 10^{8}\;\text{m/s}$.

exercises.prompt: Does motion affect the rate of a clock as measured by an observer moving with it? Does motion affect how an observer moving relative to a clock measures its rate?

answer.solution: No to the first and yes to the second. An observer moving with the clock is at rest relative to it and measures proper time, and every clock in her frame, her heartbeat included, runs at its ordinary rate, so she can detect nothing from the clock alone. An observer moving relative to the clock measures a longer time $\kdt = \gamma\kdto$ for each of its ticks, so to him the clock runs slow, by a factor that is very nearly 1 at everyday speeds and large near $\kc$.

exercises.prompt: To whom does the elapsed time for a process seem to be longer, an observer moving relative to the process or an observer moving with the process? Which observer measures proper time?

answer.solution: The elapsed time seems longer to the observer moving relative to the process, who measures $\kdt = \gamma\kdto$, and $\gamma$ is always greater than 1 for any relative motion. The observer moving with the process is at rest relative to it and measures the proper time $\kdto$, which is the shorter of the two.

exercises.prompt: How could you travel far into the future without aging significantly? Could this method also allow you to travel into the past?

answer.solution: Travel away from the Earth at a speed close to $\kc$ and come back, as the astronaut twin does. Your own clocks, your aging included, run at their ordinary rate and measure a proper time of a few years, while the Earth-bound frame measures $\gamma$ times as long; at $\gamma = 30.0$ a 2.00-year trip returns you 60.0 years into the Earth’s future. The method cannot take you into the past. Time dilation only ever makes the Earth’s elapsed time longer than yours, since $\gamma$ is never less than 1, and reaching $\gamma$ infinite would take a speed of $\kc$, which nothing with mass can reach, so no speed runs your clock backward relative to the Earth’s.

exercises.prompt: Particles called $\pi$-mesons are produced by accelerator beams. If these particles travel at $2.70\times 10^{8}\;\text{m/s}$ and live $2.60\times 10^{-8}\;\text{s}$ when at rest relative to an observer, how long do they live as viewed in the laboratory?

answer.hint: The lifetime at rest is the proper time. Find $\kv/\kc = 0.900$, then $\gamma$, and multiply.

exercises.prompt: A neutral $\pi$-meson is a particle that can be created by accelerator beams. If one such particle lives $1.40\times 10^{-16}\;\text{s}$ as measured in the laboratory, and $0.840\times 10^{-16}\;\text{s}$ when at rest relative to an observer, what is its velocity relative to the laboratory? Give it as a fraction of $\kc$.

answer.hint: The ratio of the two lifetimes is $\gamma$. Solve $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - \kv^2/\kc^2}$ for $\kv/\kc = \sqrt{1 - 1/\gamma^2}$.

exercises.prompt: If relativistic effects are to be less than 1%, then $\gamma$ must be less than 1.01. At what relative velocity is $\gamma=1.01$? Give it as a fraction of $\kc$.
(a) At what relative velocity is $\gamma=1.50$? (b) At what relative velocity is $\gamma=100$? Give each as a fraction of $\kc$.

parts.hint: The same relation; keep five digits to see how close to $\kc$ the speed must be.

exercises.prompt: Unreasonable Results. (a) Find the value of $\gamma$ for the following situation. An Earth-bound observer measures 23.9 h to have passed while signals from a high-velocity space probe indicate that 24.0 h have passed on board. (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which assumptions are unreasonable or inconsistent?

answer.hint: The time on board the probe is the proper time, so $\gamma = \kdt/\kdto$.
answer.solution:
(a) 0.996

(b) $\gamma$ cannot be less than 1.

(c) Assumption that time is longer in moving ship is unreasonable.
